architecture_decisions.title: Native mobile app (iOS Swift + Android Kotlin)
architecture_decisions.context: Platform requires geofencing, biometric auth, and push notifications — all deeply integrated with OS APIs
architecture_decisions.decision: Build native apps using Swift (iOS) and Kotlin (Android) rather than cross-platform (React Native/Flutter)
architecture_decisions.consequences: Higher development cost (two codebases) but better performance, battery optimization, and access to native geofencing/biometric APIs. Aligns with Lloyds standard.
architecture_decisions.kb_reference: kb-L0-lloyds-enterprise-architecture §3.1 (Native mobile — Swift iOS, Kotlin Android, NOT React Native)

architecture_decisions.title: Spring Boot microservices on GKE
architecture_decisions.context: Backend needs to support 1M concurrent users with 2-second delivery SLA
architecture_decisions.decision: Java Spring Boot microservices deployed as containers on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE)
architecture_decisions.consequences: Proven scalability on GKE with HPA. Spring Boot ecosystem provides OAuth2, circuit breakers (Resilience4j), and observability. Aligns with Lloyds standard.

architecture_decisions.title: Cloud SQL (PostgreSQL) for transactional data
architecture_decisions.context: Need ACID transactions for user accounts, consents, and sessions with HA failover
architecture_decisions.decision: Use Cloud SQL (PostgreSQL) with regional HA configuration for all transactional data
architecture_decisions.consequences: Automatic failover (RPO=0, RTO<60s). PostGIS extension available for Sprint 2 geofencing. Managed backups and encryption at rest.
architecture_decisions.kb_reference: kb-L0-lloyds-enterprise-architecture §3.2 (Cloud SQL PostgreSQL for transactional data)

architecture_decisions.title: Redis (Memorystore) for rate limiting and frequency capping
architecture_decisions.context: Notification frequency capping requires sub-millisecond reads within the 2-second delivery SLA
architecture_decisions.decision: Use Memorystore (Redis) for rate limiting counters, frequency cap state, and session cache
architecture_decisions.consequences: Sub-millisecond reads. HA with automatic failover. TTL-based expiry for daily resets. Adds operational complexity of a second data store.

architecture_decisions.title: JWT with refresh token rotation for session management
architecture_decisions.context: Mobile app needs persistent sessions with security against token theft
architecture_decisions.decision: Short-lived JWT access tokens (15 min) + long-lived refresh tokens (30 days) with rotation on each use
architecture_decisions.consequences: Stateless access token validation (no DB lookup per request). Refresh rotation detects token theft (reuse invalidates family). Secure enclave storage on device.

architecture_decisions.title: Immutable consent records (append-only)
architecture_decisions.context: GDPR Art. 7 requires proof of consent with timestamp and version. Consent can be withdrawn but history must be retained for audit.
architecture_decisions.decision: Consents table is append-only. New consent supersedes previous (superseded_at set). Never delete or update consent records.
architecture_decisions.consequences: Full audit trail for regulatory compliance. Slightly more complex queries (filter by superseded_at IS NULL for current state). Storage grows over time but consent records are small.

architecture_decisions.title: Pub/Sub for async event communication
architecture_decisions.context: Notification dispatch, consent changes, and audit logging should not block the user-facing request path
architecture_decisions.decision: Use Google Cloud Pub/Sub for async events: user.registered, user.verified, consent.recorded, notification.requested
architecture_decisions.consequences: Decouples services. Notification service subscribes to events independently. Guaranteed delivery with dead-letter topics. Adds eventual consistency.
architecture_decisions.kb_reference: kb-L0-lloyds-enterprise-architecture §4.1 (Pub/Sub for async messaging), §7.1 (Pub/Sub events for async communication)

architecture_decisions.title: OTP codes stored as SHA-256 hash
architecture_decisions.context: OTP codes are sensitive — if database is compromised, codes should not be usable
architecture_decisions.decision: Store OTP codes as SHA-256 hash. On verification, hash the submitted code and compare. Never store or log plaintext OTP.
architecture_decisions.consequences: Cannot recover OTP from database (one-way hash). Slightly more complex verification logic. Aligns with security best practices.

risks.risk: SMS OTP delivery delays in certain regions may exceed 10-second user expectation
risks.mitigation: Offer email as alternative delivery channel. Show 'Code not received?' after 30 seconds with option to switch. Monitor delivery latency per provider.

risks.risk: iOS push notification permission denial rate (40-60%) reduces platform value
risks.mitigation: Pre-permission screen (F-02.5) explains value before OS prompt. In-app fallback mode ensures app works without push. Track opt-in rate as KPI.

risks.risk: Redis (Memorystore) single point of failure for frequency capping
risks.mitigation: HA Redis with automatic failover. On Redis unavailability, allow notifications through (fail-open) rather than blocking all delivery.

risks.risk: Refresh token theft via device compromise
risks.mitigation: Tokens stored in OS secure enclave (Keychain/Keystore). Refresh rotation detects reuse. Password change invalidates all sessions globally.

dependency_order: EP-00 (Design System) first — all UI stories depend on component library
EP-01 F-01.1/F-01.2 (Registration + OTP) before F-01.3 (Biometric) — need account before enrollment
EP-01 F-01.4 (Consent) after F-01.2 — consent collected post-verification
EP-01 F-01.5 (Session) parallel with F-01.3 — both depend on verified account
EP-02 F-02.1 (Push integration) can start parallel with EP-01 — backend service independent
EP-02 F-02.5 (Permission request) after EP-01 F-01.4 — permission requested after consent
EP-02 F-02.2/F-02.3/F-02.4 (Preferences) after EP-01 F-01.5 — need authenticated session
reasoning: Sprint 1 establishes the complete user lifecycle foundation: account creation → verification → consent → session management, plus the notification delivery pipeline. Architecture follows Lloyds enterprise standards (GKE, Spring Boot, Cloud SQL, Pub/Sub, Memorystore). Native mobile chosen for geofencing/biometric requirements. Append-only consent for GDPR compliance. JWT rotation for mobile session security. All decisions prioritize the 2-second delivery SLA that Sprint 2's geofencing will depend on.
